;;; is_prime.lova  --  primality by trial division
;;;
;;; The first LOVA program with a real algorithm in it.  Everything in
;;; apps/ before this one was a single fixed-depth expression: the
;;; language had no functions, no recursion and no loops, so a program
;;; could only be as long as it was written.  This one recurses.
;;;
;;; Returns:
;;;   1  if n is prime
;;;   0  otherwise
;;;
;;; Three M9 pieces carry it:
;;;
;;;   `defn`       -- a named, curried function.  Sugar: it desugars to
;;;                   (let name (lambda a (lambda b body)) ...), and the
;;;                   `let` is a letrec, which is why `check` may call
;;;                   itself.
;;;   `mod`        -- 0x0C, the divisibility test.
;;;   `threshold`  -- with `deviation`, the ordering test.  There is no
;;;                   `<` operator in the 64-token core; ordering is
;;;                   built out of the surprise family:
;;;                       (a > b)  ==  (threshold (deviation a b))
;;;
;;; Recursion depth is sqrt(n), so n up to MAX_NT_INPUT stays far
;;; inside the substrate's MAX_CALL_DEPTH.

;; Has n a divisor at or above d?  Walks d upward until d*d exceeds n.
(defn check [d n]
  (if-surprise (threshold (deviation (mul d d) n))
    1                                 ; d*d > n  -- no divisor exists, prime
    (if-surprise (mod n d)
      (check (merge d 1) n)           ; n mod d != 0  -- try the next d
      0)))                            ; d divides n   -- composite

(defn is-prime [n]
  (if-surprise (threshold (deviation 2 n))
    0                                 ; 2 > n  -- 0 and 1 are not prime
    (check 2 n)))

(is-prime 1999)

;;; is_perfect.lova  --  the first real LOVA program
;;;
;;; Classify an integer n as "perfect" in the number-theoretic sense:
;;; a number is perfect iff the sum of its proper divisors equals n,
;;; i.e. sigma(n) = 2n.  Examples: 6 (1+2+3 = 6), 28, 496, 8128.
;;;
;;; Returns:
;;;   1  if n is perfect
;;;   0  otherwise
;;;
;;; The program uses `surprise` as the detector.  The naive hypothesis
;;; "if n were perfect then sigma(n) would be 2n" is encoded as the
;;; predicted value; the actual sigma(n) is computed and compared.
;;; surprise returns |predicted - actual|.  Zero surprise = perfect.
;;;
;;; This is LOVA-idiomatic: instead of `if sigma(n) == 2*n return 1`,
;;; we express the check as "how surprised are we if we assume
;;; perfection?"  The substrate emits a structured surprise event as a
;;; side effect, so the AI observer sees the comparison in the trace.

(let 0 496                                  ; bind input n as name 0

  (if-surprise

    (surprise
      (merge (ref 0) (ref 0))               ; predicted: 2n (if perfect)
      (sigma (ref 0)))                      ; actual:    sigma(n)

    0                                       ; surprise != 0  -> not perfect
    1))                                     ; surprise  = 0  -> PERFECT

;;; coprime.lova  --  are two integers coprime?
;;;
;;; Two integers are coprime iff gcd(a, b) = 1.  Simplest possible
;;; LOVA program for this: invert the gcd check via surprise.
;;;
;;; Returns:
;;;   1  if a and b are coprime (gcd = 1)
;;;   0  otherwise
;;;
;;; Observation: no `merge (ref 0) (ref 0)` trick needed here — we can
;;; just compute gcd and compare to literal 1 via surprise.  Shorter,
;;; shows that surprise is a general equality primitive in this
;;; substrate, not only a debug mechanism.

(if-surprise
  (surprise 1 (gcd 14 15))     ; surprise = |1 - gcd(a,b)|
  0                              ; non-zero surprise -> not coprime
  1)                             ; zero surprise     -> coprime

;;; collatz.lova  --  how many steps does n take to reach 1?
;;;
;;; The Collatz step: halve an even number, else 3n+1.  Iterate until
;;; the value is 1 and count the iterations.  Nobody knows whether this
;;; terminates for every n, which makes it an honest exercise of the
;;; substrate's ceilings rather than a decorative one: a program that
;;; might not stop must fail as a structured anomaly, not as a hang.
;;;
;;; Returns: the number of steps from n to 1.
;;;
;;; Two things worth noticing.
;;;
;;; 1. The counter.  LOVA has no mutable state (Constraint 4) and no
;;;    pair type, so a loop cannot carry an accumulator alongside its
;;;    value.  The accumulator is instead an extra parameter and the
;;;    iteration is recursion -- which is what currying is for:
;;;    (steps n acc) is (lambda n (lambda acc ...)) applied twice.
;;;
;;; 2. The ceiling.  Recursion depth here is the step count itself, so
;;;    a seed whose trajectory is longer than MAX_CALL_DEPTH raises a
;;;    DepthTrap.  That is the designed behaviour: n=27 takes 111 steps
;;;    and returns; n=2463 takes 208 and traps, with an anomaly naming
;;;    the limit and what to do about it.  Compare a Python version,
;;;    which would raise RecursionError with a stack trace an agent has
;;;    to parse.
;;;
;;; `loop-until` would give unbounded iteration without any call depth
;;; at all -- (apply (loop-until pred step) seed) -- but it threads a
;;; single value, so it cannot count.  It is the right tool for
;;; something like the odd part of n:
;;;     (apply (loop-until (lambda x (mod x 2))
;;;                        (lambda x (partition x))) n)

;; One Collatz step: n/2 when even, 3n+1 when odd.
;; `partition` is 0x02, which halves; `mod n 2` is the parity test.
(defn next [n]
  (if-surprise (mod n 2)
    (merge (mul 3 n) 1)               ; odd  -> 3n + 1
    (partition n)))                   ; even -> n / 2

;; Count steps until the value is 1.  `(deviation n 1)` is non-zero for
;; as long as n differs from 1, which is exactly the loop condition.
(defn steps [n acc]
  (if-surprise (deviation n 1)
    (steps (next n) (merge acc 1))
    acc))

(steps 27 0)

;;; palindrome.lova  --  is a string the same read backwards?
;;;
;;; The first LOVA program that operates on data rather than on a
;;; number.  Until M10 the only value in the language was a scalar
;;; integer: no strings, no lists, no way to return two things.  A cons
;;; cell changed that, and a string turned out to cost nothing on top of
;;; it -- `"racecar"` is surface sugar for a list of codepoints, so the
;;; token table spends no slots on strings at all.
;;;
;;; Returns:
;;;   1  if the string reads the same both ways
;;;   0  otherwise
;;;
;;; Three things worth noticing.
;;;
;;; 1. `rev` carries its accumulator as a second curried parameter --
;;;    the same pattern collatz.lova needed, for the same reason: LOVA
;;;    has no mutable state.  What is new is that the accumulator can
;;;    now be a *list*.
;;;
;;; 2. `dist` is `surprise`: |a - b|, zero exactly when two codepoints
;;;    are equal.  Equality has never needed its own operator here --
;;;    the surprise primitive was always a comparison.
;;;
;;; 3. `nil?` is the only way to see the end of a list, so every
;;;    traversal is a guarded recursion.  Taking the head of an empty
;;;    list is an error with a repair hint, not a silent zero.
;;;
;;; The short spellings (`if`, `dist`, `def`) are the one-token aliases
;;; Exp 13 measured: identical programs, 30% fewer LLM tokens.

;; Reverse a list onto an accumulator.
(def rev [xs acc]
  (if (nil? xs)
    acc
    (rev (tail xs) (cons (head xs) acc))))

;; Are two lists elementwise equal?
(def same [a b]
  (if (nil? a)
    (nil? b)                          ; a ended -- equal iff b ended too
    (if (nil? b)
      0                               ; b ended first
      (if (dist (head a) (head b))
        0                             ; heads differ
        (same (tail a) (tail b))))))  ; heads match -- keep going

(def palindrome? [s]
  (same s (rev s (nil))))

(palindrome? "racecar")

;;; tictactoe.lova  --  noughts and crosses against the substrate
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/tictactoe.lova 0
;;;   printf '5\n1\n9\n' | lova run apps/tictactoe.lova 0
;;;
;;; The argument is the board to start from, in the integer form
;;; described below; 0 is the empty board.
;;;
;;; You are X and move first; the computer is O and plays a memoised
;;; negamax, so it never loses.  Type the number of a free square, as
;;; shown on the board.  The end of the input ends the game.  The
;;; value of the program is the winner: 1 you, 2 the computer, 0 a
;;; draw or a quit.
;;;
;;; The second real program (M23; wordfreq was the first), written to
;;; find out what a turn-based game needs from the language.  What it
;;; found is in journal M23.
;;;
;;; The board is one integer in base 3: square k (0..8) is digit k, and
;;; a digit is 0 empty, 1 X, 2 O.  A program that is an integer plays
;;; on a board that is one, and the board is a map key for free.

(def powers [] (list 1 3 9 27 81 243 729 2187 6561))

(def cell [b k] (mod (div b (nth powers k)) 3))

;; Only ever called on an empty square, so adding is setting.
;; (`put` is the record macro, so the board's setter is `place`.)
(def place [b k v] (merge b (mul v (nth powers k))))

(def lines [] (list (list 0 1 2) (list 3 4 5) (list 6 7 8)
                    (list 0 3 6) (list 1 4 7) (list 2 5 8)
                    (list 0 4 8) (list 2 4 6)))

;; Who holds all three squares of a line, or 0.
(def line-owner [b l]
  (let a (cell b (nth l 0))
    (if (and (eq a (cell b (nth l 1))) (eq a (cell b (nth l 2)))) a 0)))

(def winner [b]
  (fold (lambda w (lambda l (or w (line-owner b l)))) 0 lines))

(def empties [b] (filter (lambda k (not (cell b k))) (range 0 9)))

;; What the program says about itself (M26): `lova check apps/tictactoe.lova 0`.
(example (cell 166 0) 1)                    ; X X . / . O . / . . .  -- square 1 is X
(example (cell 166 4) 2)                    ; the centre is O
(example (winner 13) 1)                     ; X on 0, 1, 2: 1 + 3 + 9
(example (winner 166) 0)
(example (len (empties 166)) 6)
(example (place 0 4 2) 162)

(def full [b] (nil? (empties b)))

(def other [p] (sub 3 p))

;; --- the search -----------------------------------------------------
;;
;; `solve` scores a position for the player about to move: 1 a forced
;; win, 0 a draw, -1 a forced loss.  Positions are memoised in a map
;; keyed by board and player, and the map is threaded through the
;; search as a value: every call returns a record `(rec score s memo
;; m)`, and the folds below carry `(rec best b move k memo m)` and read
;; their fields by name (Q84; until M24 this was `(nth st 2)`).  The
;; first move searches the whole game; every later move finds its
;; answers already there.

(def memo-key [b p] (merge (mul b 3) p))

(def solve [b p memo]
  (let known (map-get memo (memo-key b p) 5)
    (if (ne known 5)
      (rec score known memo memo)
      (let r (cond (winner b) (rec score -1 memo memo)   ; the other side just won
                   (full b)   (rec score 0 memo memo)
                   (best b p memo))
        (put r memo (map-put (get r memo) (memo-key b p) (get r score)))))))

;; The best score `p` can reach from `b`, with the memo it built.
(def best [b p memo]
  (fold (lambda st (lambda k
          (let r (solve (place b k p) (other p) (get st memo))
            (rec score (max (get st score) (neg (get r score)))
                 memo (get r memo)))))
        (rec score -2 memo memo)
        (empties b)))

;; The square to play: (rec score s move k memo m).
(def choose [b p memo]
  (fold (lambda st (lambda k
          (let r (solve (place b k p) (other p) (get st memo))
            (let sc (neg (get r score))
              (if (gt sc (get st score))
                (rec score sc move k memo (get r memo))
                (put st memo (get r memo)))))))
        (rec score -2 move -1 memo memo)
        (empties b)))

;; --- the table ------------------------------------------------------

(def glyph [b k]
  (cond (eq (cell b k) 1) "X"
        (eq (cell b k) 2) "O"
        (text-of (inc k))))

(def row [b r]
  (join (list (glyph b (mul r 3)) (glyph b (inc (mul r 3))) (glyph b (merge (mul r 3) 2))) 32))

(def show [b]
  (seq (println (row b 0)) (println (row b 1)) (println (row b 2)) (println "")))

(def announce [b]
  (let w (winner b)
    (seq (show b)
         (cond (eq w 1) (println "you win")
               (eq w 2) (println "the computer wins")
               (println "a draw"))
         w)))

;; A move from the player: a free square, or -1 at the end of the
;; input.  Anything else -- text, a taken square, a blank line -- is
;; asked again.  (Until Q78 a blank line was `nil` too, and quit.)
(def read-move [b]
  (let line (stdin)
    (if (nil? line)
      -1
      (let k (try (sub (parse-int (head (words line))) 1) -2)
        (if (and (ge k 0) (and (lt k 9) (not (cell b k))))
          k
          (seq (println "pick the number of a free square")
               (read-move b)))))))

(def play [b memo]
  (seq (show b)
       (let k (read-move b)
         (if (lt k 0)
           (seq (println "bye") 0)
           (let b2 (place b k 1)
             (if (or (winner b2) (full b2))
               (announce b2)
               (let r (choose b2 2 memo)
                 (let b3 (place b2 (get r move) 2)
                   (seq (println (join (list "the computer plays" (text-of (inc (get r move)))) 32))
                        (if (or (winner b3) (full b3))
                          (announce b3)
                          (play b3 (get r memo))))))))))))

(seq (println "you are X and move first; type the number of a square")
     (play 166 (nil)))

;;; tictactoe.lova  --  noughts and crosses against the substrate
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/tictactoe.lova 0
;;;   printf '5\n1\n9\n' | lova run apps/tictactoe.lova 0
;;;
;;; The argument is the board to start from, in the integer form
;;; described below; 0 is the empty board.
;;;
;;; You are X and move first; the computer is O and plays a memoised
;;; negamax, so it never loses.  Type the number of a free square, as
;;; shown on the board.  The end of the input ends the game.  The
;;; value of the program is the winner: 1 you, 2 the computer, 0 a
;;; draw or a quit.
;;;
;;; The second real program (M23; wordfreq was the first), written to
;;; find out what a turn-based game needs from the language.  What it
;;; found is in journal M23.
;;;
;;; The board is one integer in base 3: square k (0..8) is digit k, and
;;; a digit is 0 empty, 1 X, 2 O.  A program that is an integer plays
;;; on a board that is one, and the board is a map key for free.

(def powers [] (list 1 3 9 27 81 243 729 2187 6561))

(def cell [b k] (mod (div b (nth powers k)) 3))

;; Only ever called on an empty square, so adding is setting.
;; (`put` is the record macro, so the board's setter is `place`.)
(def place [b k v] (merge b (mul v (nth powers k))))

(def lines [] (list (list 0 1 2) (list 3 4 5) (list 6 7 8)
                    (list 0 3 6) (list 1 4 7) (list 2 5 8)
                    (list 0 4 8) (list 2 4 6)))

;; Who holds all three squares of a line, or 0.
(def line-owner [b l]
  (let a (cell b (nth l 0))
    (if (and (eq a (cell b (nth l 1))) (eq a (cell b (nth l 2)))) a 0)))

(def winner [b]
  (fold (lambda w (lambda l (or w (line-owner b l)))) 0 lines))

(def empties [b] (filter (lambda k (not (cell b k))) (range 0 9)))

;; What the program says about itself (M26): `lova check apps/tictactoe.lova 0`.
(example (cell 166 0) 1)                    ; X X . / . O . / . . .  -- square 1 is X
(example (cell 166 4) 2)                    ; the centre is O
(example (winner 13) 1)                     ; X on 0, 1, 2: 1 + 3 + 9
(example (winner 166) 0)
(example (len (empties 166)) 6)
(example (place 0 4 2) 162)

(def full [b] (nil? (empties b)))

(def other [p] (sub 3 p))

;; --- the search -----------------------------------------------------
;;
;; `solve` scores a position for the player about to move: 1 a forced
;; win, 0 a draw, -1 a forced loss.  Positions are memoised in a map
;; keyed by board and player, and the map is threaded through the
;; search as a value: every call returns a record `(rec score s memo
;; m)`, and the folds below carry `(rec best b move k memo m)` and read
;; their fields by name (Q84; until M24 this was `(nth st 2)`).  The
;; first move searches the whole game; every later move finds its
;; answers already there.

(def memo-key [b p] (merge (mul b 3) p))

(def solve [b p memo]
  (let known (map-get memo (memo-key b p) 5)
    (if (ne known 5)
      (rec score known memo memo)
      (let r (cond (winner b) (rec score -1 memo memo)   ; the other side just won
                   (full b)   (rec score 0 memo memo)
                   (best b p memo))
        (put r memo (map-put (get r memo) (memo-key b p) (get r score)))))))

;; The best score `p` can reach from `b`, with the memo it built.
(def best [b p memo]
  (fold (lambda st (lambda k
          (let r (solve (place b k p) (other p) (get st memo))
            (rec score (max (get st score) (neg (get r score)))
                 memo (get r memo)))))
        (rec score -2 memo memo)
        (empties b)))

;; The square to play: (rec score s move k memo m).
(def choose [b p memo]
  (fold (lambda st (lambda k
          (let r (solve (place b k p) (other p) (get st memo))
            (let sc (neg (get r score))
              (if (gt sc (get st score))
                (rec score sc move k memo (get r memo))
                (put st memo (get r memo)))))))
        (rec score -2 move -1 memo memo)
        (empties b)))

;; --- the table ------------------------------------------------------

(def glyph [b k]
  (cond (eq (cell b k) 1) "X"
        (eq (cell b k) 2) "O"
        (text-of (inc k))))

(def row [b r]
  (join (list (glyph b (mul r 3)) (glyph b (inc (mul r 3))) (glyph b (merge (mul r 3) 2))) 32))

(def show [b]
  (seq (println (row b 0)) (println (row b 1)) (println (row b 2)) (println "")))

(def announce [b]
  (let w (winner b)
    (seq (show b)
         (cond (eq w 1) (println "you win")
               (eq w 2) (println "the computer wins")
               (println "a draw"))
         w)))

;; A move from the player: a free square, or -1 at the end of the
;; input.  Anything else -- text, a taken square, a blank line -- is
;; asked again.  (Until Q78 a blank line was `nil` too, and quit.)
(def read-move [b]
  (let line (stdin)
    (if (nil? line)
      -1
      (let k (try (sub (parse-int (head (words line))) 1) -2)
        (if (and (ge k 0) (and (lt k 9) (not (cell b k))))
          k
          (seq (println "pick the number of a free square")
               (read-move b)))))))

(def play [b memo]
  (seq (show b)
       (let k (read-move b)
         (if (lt k 0)
           (seq (println "bye") 0)
           (let b2 (place b k 1)
             (if (or (winner b2) (full b2))
               (announce b2)
               (let r (choose b2 2 memo)
                 (let b3 (place b2 (get r move) 2)
                   (seq (println (join (list "the computer plays" (text-of (inc (get r move)))) 32))
                        (if (or (winner b3) (full b3))
                          (announce b3)
                          (play b3 (get r memo))))))))))))

(seq (println "you are X and move first; type the number of a square")
     (play 163 (nil)))

;;; logstats.lova  --  a request log, summarised per service
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/logstats.lova access.log --allow fs-read
;;;
;;; Each line of the log is "service status milliseconds", for example
;;; "api 200 123".  The program prints, per service and most requests
;;; first, the request count, the mean and maximum latency, and how
;;; many requests failed (status 400 and up).  Lines that are not
;;; three fields with two numbers are skipped.  The value of the
;;; program is the number of lines it counted.
;;;
;;; Written at M23 as the data-pipeline scenario: read, parse, group,
;;; aggregate, sort, print.  The one thing it cannot say is a mean
;;; with a decimal point: LOVA has integers only, so `div` rounds
;;; down, and a mean of 149.9 prints as 149.

;; "api 200 123" -> (list "api" 200 123), or nil for anything else.
(def parse [line]
  (let ws (words line)
    (if (lt (len ws) 3)
      (nil)
      (try (list (nth ws 0) (parse-int (nth ws 1)) (parse-int (nth ws 2)))
           (nil)))))

;; The running figures for a service: (list count total-ms max-ms errors).
(def update [stats r]
  (let old (map-get stats (head r) (list 0 0 0 0))
    (let status (nth r 1)
      (let ms (nth r 2)
        (map-put stats (head r)
                 (list (inc (head old))
                       (merge (nth old 1) ms)
                       (max (nth old 2) ms)
                       (merge (nth old 3) (if (ge status 400) 1 0))))))))

;; Most requests first.  A map pair is (list key value).
(def by-count [a b]
  (ge (head (head (tail a))) (head (head (tail b)))))

(def show [e]
  (let v (head (tail e))
    (println (join (list (head e)
                         (text-of (head v))
                         (text-of (div (nth v 1) (head v)))
                         (text-of (nth v 2))
                         (text-of (nth v 3)))
                   32))))

(boundary "fs-read"
  (let records (filter (lambda r (not (nil? r)))
                       (map parse (lines (fs-read "corpus/golden/fixtures/sample.log"))))
    (let stats (fold update (nil) records)
      (seq (println "service requests mean-ms max-ms errors")
           (map show (sort-by by-count (map-pairs stats)))
           (len records)))))

;;; sandbox.lova  --  run untrusted programs, one per line, and report
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/sandbox.lova 5000 < programs.txt
;;;
;;; Each line of the input is a LOVA program in the text surface.  The
;;; sandbox reads it into a program value, runs it under a budget of
;;; the given number of nodes, and prints one line: the program's
;;; digest (its integer, folded to eighteen digits -- Q80), and either
;;; its value or the fault it raised, by name.  A
;;; program that loops for ever meets the budget; one that reads a
;;; file meets the boundary it did not declare; one that is not even
;;; a program is reported as such.  Nothing a line can do reaches the
;;; sandbox: every fault is an anomaly with a code, and the handler
;;; turns the code into a word.  The value of the program is the
;;; number of lines that produced a value.
;;;
;;; Written at M23 as the agent scenario: the host that runs code an
;;; agent wrote is itself a LOVA program, and needs no grant at all.

(def fault-name [code]
  (cond (eq code 1) "budget exceeded"
        (eq code 2) "recursion too deep"
        (eq code 3) "conservation violated"
        (eq code 4) "domain error"
        (eq code 5) "type violation"
        (eq code 6) "unbound reference"
        (eq code 7) "not a program"
        (eq code 9) "capability denied"
        (eq code 10) "signalled"
        (append "signal " (text-of code))))

;; The value as text; a list or a function has none, and says so.
(def value-text [v]
  (try (text-of v) "a value that is not a number"))

;; One line: 1 if the program produced a value, else 0.
(def run-line [line]
  (let report (when-anomaly
                (let p (read line)
                  (let v (budget 5000 (eval p))
                    (list 1 (append (text-of (digest p)) (append " => " (value-text v))))))
                (lambda code (list 0 (append "fault: " (fault-name code)))))
    (seq (println (head (tail report)))
         (head report))))

(def run-all [count]
  (let line (stdin)
    (cond (nil? line) count
          (nil? (words line)) (run-all count)          ; a blank line is not a program
          (run-all (merge count (run-line line))))))

;;; batch.lova  --  a batch of jobs, each under its own cost contract
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/batch.lova 300 2000
;;;
;;; For every n from 1 to the first argument, count the Collatz steps
;;; to 1 -- but each job may spend at most the second argument in
;;; nodes.  A job that would cost more is stopped by its `budget`, the
;;; anomaly is caught, and the job is recorded as over budget rather
;;; than left to run.  The batch prints how many jobs finished, how
;;; many were over budget, and the longest trajectory among those that
;;; finished.  The value of the program is the number that finished.
;;;
;;; Written at M23 as the cost-contract scenario: Axiom 4 (conservation
;;; is declared in the program, not policed outside it) as something
;;; a program uses per job, so a batch survives its expensive items
;;; and says which they were.

;; The arguments, declared first: a `{placeholder}` is filled from the
;; command line in the order of its first appearance in the code.
(def jobs [] 300)
(def cost [] 2000)

(def next [n] (if (mod n 2) (merge (mul 3 n) 1) (div n 2)))

(def steps [n acc]
  (if (eq n 1) acc (steps (next n) (inc acc))))

;; The step count, or -1 when the job ran out of budget.
(def job [n]
  (when-anomaly (budget cost (steps n 0))
                (lambda code -1)))

(def finished [rs] (filter (lambda r (ge r 0)) rs))

(let results (map job (range 1 (inc jobs)))
  (let done (finished results)
    (seq (println (join (list "finished:" (text-of (len done))) 32))
         (println (join (list "over budget:" (text-of (sub (len results) (len done)))) 32))
         (println (join (list "longest:" (text-of (fold (lambda a (lambda b (max a b))) 0 done))) 32))
         (len done))))

;;; repair.lova  --  a program that repairs another program
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/repair.lova 55 30 200
;;;
;;; The patient is `(merge (mul 6 9) 1)`, which is 55 when it should be
;;; the target given as the first argument -- but the target is yours
;;; to choose, so make the patient wrong by choosing anything else.
;;; The contract is `conserve`: the patient's value must equal the
;;; target, and a run that does not is a conservation anomaly (code
;;; 3), which the repairer catches.  On each failure it mutates the
;;; patient -- a literal nudged, an operator swapped -- at the
;;; strength given as the second argument, keeps the mutation only if
;;; it brings the value closer (the surprise is the signal), tries up
;;; to the number of attempts given as the third, and stops at the
;;; first version that satisfies the contract.  It then prints the fixed text, how many
;;; attempts it took, and the fix's line of descent back to the
;;; original.  The value of the program is the attempts used, or 0 if
;;; the budget of attempts ran out.
;;;
;;; Written at M23 as the self-repair scenario: Axiom 7 (a deviation is
;;; a structured anomaly) driving Axiom 6's `mutate`, with Axiom 5's
;;; lineage recording every step.  Nothing here is Python.

;; The arguments, declared first: a `{placeholder}` is filled from the
;; command line in the order of its first appearance in the code.
(def target [] 42)
(def strength [] 30)
(def attempts [] 200)

(def line [label v] (println (join (list label v) 32)))

;; 1 when `p` meets the contract, 0 when it violates it or faults.
(def holds [p]
  (when-anomaly (seq (conserve target (eval p)) 1)
                (lambda code 0)))

;; How far `p` is from the contract: the surprise of its value against
;; the target, or a large number if it faults.  This is the signal that
;; guides the repair (Axiom 7): a mutation is kept only if it shrinks it.
(def gap [p]
  (when-anomaly (surprise target (eval p))
                (lambda code 1000000)))

(def attempt [p n]
  (cond (holds p)
          (seq (line "fixed:" (explain p))
               (line "attempts:" (text-of n))
               (line "descent:" (text-of (len (lineage-query p))))
               (line "why:" (why p))
               n)
        (ge n attempts)
          (seq (line "gave up after" (text-of n)) 0)
        (let candidate (mutate p strength)
          (attempt (if (lt (gap candidate) (gap p)) candidate p) (inc n)))))

(let patient (quote (merge (mul 6 9) 1))
  (seq (line "patient:" (explain patient))
       (line "target:" (text-of target))
       (attempt patient 0)))

;;; evolve.lova  --  a function is a population; watch it converge
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/evolve.lova 1000 40
;;;
;;; Five arithmetic programs are seeded into a pool whose fitness is
;;; the distance from the target given as the first argument.  The
;;; pool is evolved for the number of generations given as the
;;; second: each round retires the least fit, clones and mutates the
;;; fittest.  Then the winner is asked to account for itself -- its
;;; text, its value, its generation, why it exists, and how long its
;;; line of descent is -- all from inside the language.  The value of
;;; the program is the winner's remaining distance from the target.
;;;
;;; Written at M23 as the evolution scenario: Axiom 6 (a function is
;;; a pool of variants) and Axiom 5 (provenance is intrinsic) in one
;;; program, with `lib/evolution.lova` supplying the helpers.

(use "evolution")

(def score [] (lambda p (surprise 42 (eval p))))

(def line [label v] (println (join (list label v) 32)))

(let pool (evolve-n (defpop score
                      (quote (mul 7 8))
                      (quote (merge 100 (mul 3 3)))
                      (quote (sigma 12))
                      (quote (mul (p 5) (tau 12)))
                      (quote (merge (mul 20 20) 1)))
                    60)
  (let winner (best pool)
    (seq (line "winner:" (explain winner))
         (line "value:" (text-of (eval winner)))
         (line "distance:" (text-of (best-score pool)))
         (line "generation:" (text-of (generation winner)))
         (line "why:" (why winner))
         (line "ancestors:" (text-of (len (lineage-query winner))))
         (best-score pool))))

value: 42
distance: 0
generation: 0
why: root quoted

;;; tanks.lova  --  tank battle in a terminal, turn by turn
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/tanks.lova 7
;;;   printf 'f\nw\nw\nf\n' | lova run apps/tanks.lova 7
;;;
;;; The argument seeds the enemies' wandering.  Each line you type is
;;; one turn: w / d / s / a move (and turn to face) up / right / down /
;;; left, f fires, an empty line waits, q quits.  Every enemy moves and
;;; every bullet flies two cells after your move.  Eight enemies arrive
;;; along the top row, up to three at a time; destroy them all before
;;; one of them destroys you or the base `@` beside you.  The value of
;;; the program is your score.
;;;
;;; The rules are `lib/tanks.lova`; this file is the terminal.  The
;;; same rules run in real time in a window: `python apps/tanks/tank_game.py`.

(use "tanks")

(def show [w]
  (seq (println (render w))
       (println (join (list "turn" (text-of (get w turn))
                            "score" (text-of (get w score))
                            "enemies left" (text-of (enemies-left w)))
                      32))
       (println "")))

;; The next command: w d s a f, an empty line to wait, q or the end of
;; the input to quit.  Anything else is a wait too.  (`w` is unused: a
;; def without a parameter is a constant, computed once, and this must
;; read a line every turn.)
(def read-cmd [w]
  (let line (stdin)
    (if (nil? line)
      -1
      (let c (head line)
        (cond (eq c 119) 1
              (eq c 100) 2
              (eq c 115) 3
              (eq c 97) 4
              (eq c 102) 5
              (eq c 113) -1
              0)))))

(def one-turn [w]
  (seq (show w)
       (let c (read-cmd w)
         (if (lt c 0) (put w quit 1) (step w c)))))

(def over [w] (or (get w status) (map-get w "quit" 0)))

(def finish [w]
  (seq (if (get w status) (show w) 0)
       (println (cond (eq (get w status) 1) "you win: the last enemy is gone"
                      (eq (get w status) 2) "you were hit"
                      (eq (get w status) 3) "the base fell"
                      "bye"))
       (get w score)))

(seq (println "w d s a move, f fires, Enter waits, q quits")
     (finish (iterate (new-game 7) over one-turn)))

;;; maze.lova  --  a first-person 3D maze in a terminal, a line a turn
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/maze.lova 0
;;;   printf 'wwww\nd\nww\n' | lova run apps/maze.lova 0
;;;
;;; Each line you type is a run of moves, played in order, and then the
;;; view is drawn: `w` forward, `s` back, `a` turn left, `d` turn
;;; right, `z` and `x` step sideways, an empty line waits, `q` quits.
;;; So `wwwd` walks three steps and turns.  The argument is which way
;;; you face at the start.
;;;
;;; Six orbs are scattered in the maze; carry all six to the door in
;;; the south-east and it opens.  The value of the program is the
;;; number of moves it took you.
;;;
;;; The maze, the walking and the casting are `lib/ray.lova`; this file
;;; is the terminal, and everything in it turns a `frame` -- a list of
;;; columns and a list of orb columns, which the library computes
;;; without knowing what a character is -- into text.  The same rules
;;; run in real time in a window: `python apps/maze/maze3d.py`.

(use "ray")

(def SW [] 60)                          ; columns of view
(def ROWS [] 22)                        ; rows of view
(def MID [] 11)                         ; the horizon

;; Near to far.  A wall further away is written with a lighter mark,
;; and a wall you see edge-on (the `s` of a column) one lighter still,
;; which is the whole of the lighting model.
(def ramp [] "@#%=+:-.")

(def shade [d side]
  (nth ramp (min 7 (merge (div d ONE) (if side 1 0)))))

;; The floor: a row near the bottom of the screen is floor close to
;; your feet, a row near the horizon is floor far away.
(def floor-char [y]
  (nth ramp (min 7 (merge 3 (div MID (max 1 (sub y MID)))))))


;; The ceiling is dark: a blank above the horizon is what makes a wall
;; unmistakable in characters.

;; --- one row of the picture -----------------------------------------

(def NO-ORB [] (rec t 0 u 0 d 0))

(def cell-char [cols orbs x y]
  (let o (map-get orbs x NO-ORB)
    (if (and (ge y (get o t)) (lt y (get o u)))
      (if (lt (get o d) 2048) 79 111)   ; O near, o far
      (let c (nth cols x)
        (let h (get c h)
          (let top (div (sub ROWS h) 2)
            (cond (and (ge y top) (lt y (merge top h))) (shade (get c d) (get c s))
                  (lt y MID) 32
                  (floor-char y))))))))

(def row-text [cols orbs y]
  (text-of-chars (map (lambda x (cell-char cols orbs x y)) (range 0 SW))))

;; --- the map in the corner ------------------------------------------
;;
;; Nine rows of the maze around you, drawn beside the first nine rows
;; of the view: `A` is you (pointing the way you face), `o` an orb,
;; `D` the door, `#` a wall.

(def facing [w] (nth "ESWN" (mod (div (merge (mul 2 (get w ang)) 64) 128) 4)))

(def map-char [w cx cy]
  (cond (and (eq cx (div (get w px) ONE)) (eq cy (div (get w py) ONE))) (facing w)
        (any (lambda o (and (eq (get o x) cx) (eq (get o y) cy))) (orbs-live w)) 111
        (eq (wall-at cx cy) DOOR) 68
        (wall-at cx cy) 35
        46))

(def map-row [w y]
  (let cy (merge (sub (div (get w py) ONE) 4) y)
    (text-of-chars (map (lambda i (map-char w (merge (sub (div (get w px) ONE) 4) i) cy))
                        (range 0 9)))))

;; --- the screen -----------------------------------------------------

(def orb-map [f]
  (fold (lambda m (lambda s (map-put m (get s c) s))) (nil) (get f spr)))

(def screen [w]
  (let f (frame w SW ROWS)
    (let cols (get f cols)
      (let orbs (orb-map f)
        (join (map (lambda y
                     (let line (row-text cols orbs y)
                       (if (lt y 9)
                         (join (list line (map-row w y)) "  ")
                         line)))
                   (range 0 ROWS))
              10)))))

(def show [w]
  (seq (println (screen w))
       (println (join (list "orbs left" (text-of (orbs-left w))
                            " ticks" (text-of (get w turn))
                            " facing" (text-of-chars (list (facing w)))
                            (get w msg))
                      "  "))
       (println "")))

;; --- the loop -------------------------------------------------------

;;; cube.lova  --  a cube turning in three dimensions, drawn in characters
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/cube.lova
;;;   printf '\n\n\n\n' | lova run apps/cube.lova
;;;
;;; Press Enter to turn it one step, a digit to turn it that many, `q`
;;; to stop.  The value of the program is the number of steps you
;;; turned it.
;;;
;;; The maze next door is a raycaster -- a picture built out of a plan.
;;; This is the other kind of 3D and the one that has to be said out
;;; loud: eight corners with three coordinates each, turned about two
;;; axes by a rotation, moved away from the camera, and divided by
;;; their depth.  Nothing about it is special to a grid.  It is here
;;; because LOVA has no floating point and the interesting question was
;;; whether that costs it the geometry; `lib/fixed.lova` is the answer,
;;; and this file and `lib/ray.lova` are the two uses of it.
;;;
;;; The edge nearest you is written `@` and the one furthest `.`, which
;;; is the only depth cue a terminal gives you.

(use "fixed")

(def W [] 62)                           ; columns
(def H [] 25)                           ; rows
(def CX [] 31)
(def CY [] 12)
(def FOCX [] 30)                        ; columns across one unit at one unit out
(def FOCY [] 13)                        ; and rows -- half, because a character
                                        ; is about twice as tall as it is wide
(def DEPTH [] 4096)                     ; the camera stands four units back
(def SPIN [] 5)                         ; a step of the turn, about 7 degrees

;; --- the solid ------------------------------------------------------
;;
;; The eight corners of a cube of side two, and the twelve edges as
;; pairs of corner numbers.  Corner n has x negative when bit 0 is
;; clear, y when bit 1 is, z when bit 2 is.

(def corners []
  (map (lambda n (rec x (if (mod n 2) ONE (neg ONE))
                      y (if (mod (div n 2) 2) ONE (neg ONE))
                      z (if (mod (div n 4) 2) ONE (neg ONE))))
       (range 0 8)))

(def edges []
  (list (list 0 1) (list 1 3) (list 3 2) (list 2 0)
        (list 4 5) (list 5 7) (list 7 6) (list 6 4)
        (list 0 4) (list 1 5) (list 2 6) (list 3 7)))

;; --- turning it -----------------------------------------------------
;;
;; About the vertical axis by `a`, then about the horizontal by `b`.
;; Every product of two fixed-point numbers is divided by ONE to bring
;; it back to the unit; that is the whole of the discipline.

(def spin [v a b]
  (let ca (cos a)
    (let sa (sin a)
      (let x1 (div (merge (mul (get v x) ca) (mul (get v z) sa)) ONE)
        (let z1 (div (sub (mul (get v z) ca) (mul (get v x) sa)) ONE)
          (let cb (cos b)
            (let sb (sin b)
              (let y1 (div (sub (mul (get v y) cb) (mul z1 sb)) ONE)
                (let z2 (div (merge (mul (get v y) sb) (mul z1 cb)) ONE)
                  (rec x x1 y y1 z (merge z2 DEPTH)))))))))))

;; The perspective divide: a point twice as far away is half as far
;; from the middle of the screen.  `z` is never zero -- the camera
;; stands four units back and the cube reaches one and three quarters.
(def project [v]
  (rec c (merge CX (div (mul (get v x) FOCX) (get v z)))
       r (sub CY (div (mul (get v y) FOCY) (get v z)))
       z (get v z)))

;; --- drawing it -----------------------------------------------------

(def ramp [] "@#%=+:-.")

;; Nearest is `@`, furthest `.`: z runs from DEPTH - ONE to DEPTH + ONE.
(def depth-char [z]
  (nth ramp (max 0 (min 7 (div (sub z (sub DEPTH ONE)) 256)))))

(def plot [screen p]
  (if (and (and (ge (get p c) 0) (lt (get p c) W))
           (and (ge (get p r) 0) (lt (get p r) H)))
    (map-put screen (merge (mul (get p r) W) (get p c)) (depth-char (get p z)))
    screen))

;; A segment, sampled at as many points as it is long in characters --
;; one point a character is enough to leave no gaps.
(def line [screen p q]
  (let n (max 1 (max (abs (sub (get q c) (get p c)))
                     (abs (sub (get q r) (get p r)))))
    (fold (lambda s (lambda i
            (plot s (rec c (merge (get p c) (div (mul (sub (get q c) (get p c)) i) n))
                         r (merge (get p r) (div (mul (sub (get q r) (get p r)) i) n))
                         z (merge (get p z) (div (mul (sub (get q z) (get p z)) i) n))))))
          screen (range 0 (inc n)))))

(def draw [a b]
  (let ps (map (lambda v (project (spin v a b))) corners)
    (fold (lambda s (lambda e (line s (nth ps (head e)) (nth ps (last e)))))
          (nil) edges)))

(def row-text [screen r]
  (text-of-chars (map (lambda c (map-get screen (merge (mul r W) c) 32)) (range 0 W))))

(def picture [a b]
  (let screen (draw a b)
    (join (map (lambda r (row-text screen r)) (range 0 H)) 10)))

;; --- the loop -------------------------------------------------------
;;
;; The cursor home escape, so each picture is drawn over the last one
;; rather than under it.  A terminal that does not know the escape
;; prints the frames one below another, which is a flipbook and no
;; worse than it sounds.

(def home [] (text-of-chars (list 27 91 72 27 91 74)))

(def show [w]
  (seq (stdout home)
       (println (picture (get w a) (get w b)))
       (println (join (list "turn" (text-of (get w a)) "of" (text-of TURN)
                            " tilt" (text-of (get w b))
                            " -- Enter turns it, a digit turns it that far, q stops")
                      32))))

;; A line: `q` stops, a digit is that many steps, anything else is one.
(def steps-of [line]
  (cond (contains line 113) -1
        (and (not (nil? line)) (digit (head line))) (sub (head line) 48)
        1))

(def one-turn [w]
  (seq (show w)
       ;; the end of the input, not an empty line: `stdin` keeps the
       ;; terminator, so the test has to come before `chomp` takes it off
       (let raw (stdin)
         (if (nil? raw)
           (put w quit 1)
           (let n (steps-of (chomp raw))
             (if (lt n 0)
               (put w quit 1)
               (put (put (put w a (mod (merge (get w a) (mul n SPIN)) TURN))
                         b (mod (merge (get w b) (mul n 2)) TURN))
                    turn (merge (get w turn) n))))))))

(def over [w] (map-get w "quit" 0))

(seq (stdout (text-of-chars (list 27 91 50 74)))     ; clear the screen
     (get (iterate (rec a 28 b 20 turn 0) over one-turn) turn))

;;; g2048.lova  --  2048 in a terminal
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/g2048.lova 7
;;;   printf 'a\ns\na\ns\n' | lova run apps/g2048.lova 7
;;;
;;; `w a s d` (or `k h j l`) push the tiles up, left, down, right; `q`
;;; stops; several on a line are played in order, so `aassdd` is six
;;; moves.  The argument is the seed, and the same seed is the same
;;; game every time.  The value of the program is your score.
;;;
;;; The rules are `lib/g2048.lova`, a port of gabrielecirulli/2048
;;; (MIT); this file is the terminal, and the window is
;;; `python apps/g2048/game2048.py`.

(use "g2048")

;; A cell, four characters wide and right-aligned, as the original's
;; grid is square and this one has to be square in characters.
(def cell [v] (let t (if v (text-of v) ".")
                (text-cat (text-of-chars (repeat 32 (sub 5 (len t)))) t)))

(def line [row] (join (map cell row) ""))

(def show [w]
  (seq (println "")
       (println (join (map line (rows w)) 10))
       (println (join (list "" "score" (text-of (get w score))
                            " moves" (text-of (get w turn))
                            " best tile" (text-of (biggest w)))
                      32))))

(def cmd-of [c]
  (cond (or (eq c 119) (eq c 107)) 0     ; w k  up
        (or (eq c 100) (eq c 108)) 1     ; d l  right
        (or (eq c 115) (eq c 106)) 2     ; s j  down
        (or (eq c 97) (eq c 104)) 3      ; a h  left
        -1))

(def play [w cs]
  (fold (lambda ww (lambda c (let d (cmd-of c) (if (lt d 0) ww (move ww d))))) w cs))

(def one-turn [w]
  (seq (show w)
       ;; the end of the input, not an empty line: `stdin` keeps the
       ;; terminator, so the test comes before `chomp` takes it off
       (let raw (stdin)
         (if (nil? raw)
           (put w quit 1)
           (let cs (take 16 (chomp raw))
             (if (contains cs 113)
               (put w quit 1)
               (play (if (get w won) (keep-playing w) w) cs)))))))

(def over [w] (or (get w over) (map-get w "quit" 0)))

(def finish [w]
  (seq (if (get w over) (show w) 0)
       (println (cond (get w over) "no move left -- that is the game"
                      (get w won) "2048 -- and still going"
                      "bye"))
       (get w score)))

(seq (println "2048: w a s d move, q stops, several to a line")
     (finish (iterate (new-game 7) over one-turn)))

;;; fleet.lova  --  a fleet health report, from a recorded sweep
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/fleet.lova apps/fleet/sweep.txt --allow fs-read
;;;
;;; The policy is `lib/fleet.lova`, taken from RemoteX (`D:/SSH/RemoteX`,
;;; an SSH fleet manager with 38 MCP tools): its `healthCheck` parse,
;;; exactly, and the judgement it does not have -- what counts as
;;; unhealthy, in one place, for the whole fleet at once.
;;;
;;; This file connects to nothing.  It reads a file of *recorded*
;;; output, one block a machine, because a policy that decides whether
;;; two hundred production servers are in trouble should be testable
;;; without touching two hundred production servers.  The host that
;;; holds the SSH sockets hands the same text to the same function.
;;;
;;; That is also the shape of the safety argument.  `fs-read` is
;;; declared here and granted by whoever runs it; nothing in
;;; `lib/fleet.lova` can reach a socket, a file or a clock, and the
;;; compiler refuses it before the run rather than trusting it during
;;; one.

(use "fleet")

;; --- the recording --------------------------------------------------
;;
;; `--- name` on a line of its own, then that machine's output, until
;; the next one.  What `ssh_batch_health_check` collects, written down.

(def MARK [] "--- ")

(def chunk-of [block]
  (let cut (text-find block "\n")
    (if (lt cut 0)
      (list (text-trim block) "")
      (list (text-trim (text-slice block 0 cut))
            (text-slice block (inc cut) (len block))))))

(def sweep-of [raw]
  (map chunk-of (filter (lambda b (not (nil? (text-trim b)))) (text-split raw MARK))))

;; --- saying it ------------------------------------------------------

(def pad [s n]
  (if (ge (len s) n) s (text-cat s (text-of-chars (repeat 32 (sub n (len s)))))))

(def lpad [s n]
  (if (ge (len s) n) s (text-cat (text-of-chars (repeat 32 (sub n (len s)))) s)))

;; A reading in tenths, as the number a person reads: 123 is `12.3`.
(def show-tenths [v]
  (if (lt v 0) "  --" (join (list (text-of (div v 10)) (text-of (mod v 10))) ".")))

(def show-hundredths [v]
  (if (lt v 0) "  --" (join (list (text-of (div v 100)) (lpad (text-of (mod v 100)) 2)) ".")))

(def badge [w]
  (cond (eq w 2) "ALARM" (eq w 1) " warn" (eq w 3) "  ?  " "   ok"))

(def line-of [r]
  (join (list (badge (get r worst))
              (pad (get r name) 14)
              (text-cat "cpu " (lpad (show-tenths (get r cpu)) 6))
              (text-cat "mem " (lpad (show-tenths (get r mem)) 6))
              (text-cat "disk " (lpad (show-tenths (get r disk)) 6))
              (text-cat "load " (lpad (show-hundredths (get r load)) 6))
              (get r up))
        "  "))

(def summary [rep]
  (join (list (text-of (get rep total)) "machines:"
              (text-of (get rep alarm)) "alarm,"
              (text-of (get rep warn)) "warn,"
              (text-of (get rep quiet)) "ok,"
              (text-of (get rep mute)) "silent")
        32))

(boundary "fs-read"
  (def sweep [] (fs-read "apps/fleet/sweep.txt"))

  (let rep (fleet-report (sweep-of sweep))
    (seq (println "  the fleet, worst first")
         (println "")
         (println (join (map line-of (get rep rows)) 10))
         (println "")
         (println (text-cat "  " (summary rep)))
         (merge (mul 100 (get rep alarm)) (get rep warn)))))

;;; guess.lova  --  guess the number
;;;
;;;   lova run apps/guess.lova 100 --allow clock

;;; smallest interactive program needs: a source of randomness (the
;;; clock, under a declared boundary -- the program says it reads the
;;; clock and the host has to allow it), a line of input parsed as a
;;; number with the failure caught, and a loop that counts.

;; The parameter is a dummy: `(def f [] ...)` is a *constant*, evaluated
;; once where it is defined -- this one would read a line at definition
;; and then fail on its own recursive reference (Q79).  A function that
;; takes nothing still has to take something.
(def read-guess [again]
  (let line (stdin)
    (if (nil? line)
      0
      (try (parse-int (head (words line)))
           (seq (println "a number, please") (read-guess 0))))))

  (let g (read-guess 0)
    (cond (eq g 0) (seq (println "bye") 0)
          (lt g target) (seq (println "higher") (play target (inc count)))
          (gt g target) (seq (println "lower") (play target (inc count)))
          (seq (println (join (list "yes, in" (text-of (inc count)) "guesses") 32))
               (inc count)))))

;; because it is written inside the boundary that declares it.

  (seq (println (join (list "I am thinking of a number from 1 to" (text-of 3)) 32))
